newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. envoy Ekeus in Baghdad for more arms talks.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy Ekeus in Baghdad for more arms talks.

text.p: Chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus arrived in Baghdad on Thursday for more disarmament talks with Iraqi leaders.

A U.N. source in Baghdad said Ekeus, a former Swedish diplomat, was to meet Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz and other senior officials later in the evening in his latest bid to rid Iraq of weapons of mass destruction.

He said Ekeus was accompanied by international experts in all weapons areas -- nuclear, biological, chemical and ballistic missiles spheres -- including four chemical experts who conducted lengthy talks with the Iraqi side last month.
Ekeus heads the United Nations Special Commission (UNSCOM) overseeing the destruction of Iraq's lethal weapons under the terms which ended the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait.

A clean bill of health from UNSCOM is a key prerequisite for the lifting of the curbs on Iraqi oil exports. Iraq's oil-for- food deal with the United Nations under which it is allowed limited sales worth $2 billion in six months is exempt from the sanctions imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
UNSCOM is not yet satisfied it has received a full accounting of Iraq's chemical, biological and ballistic weapons programmes or evidence that all forbidden weapons have been destroyed.
Iraq says it has done all that is required from it under the Gulf War ceasefire to have the embargo on its oil lifted totally.

The visit is the latest in a series Ekeus conducts every two months to register progress of disarmament activities in Iraq. He is due to submit a six-monthly report to the Security Council around April 10.
The Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency must give similar clearance regarding Baghdad's nuclear arms capacity before the Security Council can consider lifting the oil embargo.
When Ekeus last visited Iraq in February he obtained Baghdad's long-delayed agreement for a large number of missile engines to be sent to the United States for analysis.

Iraq scrapped and buried the engines without U.N. supervision in 1992. UNSCOM is having them tested to determine whether any forbidden missiles -- those with a range greater than 150 km (93 miles) -- remain unaccounted for.
